introduction: Are the Founders of the religions equal, or do they differ? The Bahá’í answer is both, and these readings give the terms. In the station of unity all the Manifestations speak from one Source and may be called by one name. In the station of distinction each has his own individuality, mission, book and measure of revelation, fitted to the capacity of his age: the same sun in different mirrors, or at different points of the horizon, or in different months. Bahá’u’lláh rests this on two verses of the Qur’án, both given here: “some of whom We have caused to excel others” and “we make no distinction between any of His messengers.” The Gospels and Paul supply the idea of teaching measured to the hearer, and Jesus’ own sayings on unity with and subordination to the Father. Rúmí, the Gita and Guru Gobind Singh speak from other traditions. The contrasts are the claims of finality and uniqueness that each community makes for its own: the Nicene Creed, “none other name,” the Seal of the Prophets, Hebrews on the better covenant, and Chesterton’s denial that the religions teach one thing.
questions: “Some of whom We have caused to excel others” and “we make no distinction between any of His messengers.” How does the distinction between two stations let both be true?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says the differences between the Manifestations lie “in the evolutionary stages of the peoples whom they taught.” What in the Gospels and in Paul supports that, and what would a believer in each religion find hard in it?
The Nicene Creed, “none other name,” and the Seal of the Prophets each claim something unique. State what each claim protects for its community. What do the readings keep of it?
The readings do rank revelations by intensity, and place Christ and Bahá’u’lláh especially high. How is that different from the claims of superiority the readings criticize?
Chesterton says the religions differ most in what they teach. Choose one teaching on which two religions seem to disagree and try ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s explanation on it.

outside.why: “Different mirrors … but that which is reflected in these mirrors is one and the same sun.” Rúmí: the lamps are different, but the Light is the same: it comes from Beyond.

One sun in many mirrors. The creed most Christians recite sets one of them apart from all the rest: the only-begotten of his Father, God of God, Light of Light, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father. What in ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s image can a Nicene Christian accept, and where does the creed say more?

The sun rises at a different point each season, and the watcher must look where it is. The Qur’án on looking at every horizon: we believe in that which was revealed unto Abraham, and that which Moses and Jesus received, and that which the prophets received from their Lord.
The Prophets “only differ in the intensity of their revelation.” Bahá’u’lláh quotes this verse: of those messengers, some of whom We have caused to excel others.
The same chapter of the Qur’án also says: we make no distinction between any of His messengers. Bahá’u’lláh’s two stations, unity and distinction, are his reading of how both verses are true.
A difference of “comparative potency of their light.” Paul: there is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon; for one star differeth from another star in glory.
Jesus compared ranks too, and then overturned the comparison: there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist: notwithstanding he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.
Their unity lies in this, that “they judged by His command and spoke by His leave.” Jesus: I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say.
Unity of station while the persons differ. Jesus of John the Baptist: if ye will receive it, this is Elias, which was for to come.
The laws “have proceeded from one Source” and differ with the needs of their ages. Jesus: think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
Why a law may change while its Giver does not: the sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath.
“The words, deeds, religion, way and commandments of each one were different.” The Qur’án: for each We have appointed a divine law and a traced-out way.

Moses “brought forth a Book and established ordinances,” and prophets after him promulgated his law. The last lines of the Torah: there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face.

They only “appear to vary in their greatness,” because each bore a distinct message. The Letter to the Hebrews argues a real superiority of Christ over Moses: he hath obtained a more excellent ministry, the mediator of a better covenant. Is the difference between a better covenant and a greater messenger one the readings would grant?

“One branch bears fruit and others are not laden so abundantly.” The Qur’án has the same picture of difference from one source: date-palms, like and unlike, which are watered with one water. And We have made some of them to excel others in fruit.

“To the Jews Moses is the last … to the Muslims it is Muḥammad.” The verse on which the Muslim conviction rests: he is the messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says the differences “are only those of names.” What would a Muslim reader say is more than a name here?

And the Christian conviction, in Peter’s words: neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved. How do the readings ask each community to hold its own Messenger without calling him the last?

“If these names are set aside, it is evident that their aim is one.” Chesterton thought that was exactly backwards: the religions of the earth do not greatly differ in rites and forms; they do greatly differ in what they teach. What would have to be shown to answer him?
The differences were “in the evolutionary stages of the peoples whom they taught.” Jesus to his own disciples: I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now.
Paul to a young church: I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it.
Adam as childhood, Moses the teacher of outward things, Christ of the spiritual. Paul: the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ.
Paul on growing up: when I was a child, I spake as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
Greater Manifestations are preceded by heralds. The best-known herald: he must increase, but I must decrease.
“The Word as reflected in Jesus has a special meaning.” John: the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory.
Christ and Bahá’u’lláh “have appeared with a revelation beyond all conception.” Jesus’ largest saying about himself: before Abraham was, I am.
A reality that returns under different names. Krishna: I rise, from age to age, and take visible shape, and move a man with men.
He who holds the destinies of all things “is but a vassal dependent upon Thee.” Jesus: my Father is greater than I.
The Qur’án of Jesus: the Messiah, son of Mary, was no other than a messenger, messengers the like of whom had passed away before him.
Guru Gobind Singh of himself: all who call me the Supreme Being shall fall into the pit of hell. Recognize me as God’s servant only.

“All Prophets can be regarded as Sons of God.” Jesus defended his own title from a psalm that gives it more widely: is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods? If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came.
